title: Speculative Decoding (vLLM docs, latest)
quote: vLLM does not currently guarantee stable token log probabilities (logprobs).
proves: vLLM lists EAGLE, LiLiCorr, MTP, draft model, PARD, n-gram, suffix, hidden-state extraction, custom proposer, dynamic SD, adaptive verification, lossy FLy verification and per-request acceptance metrics as spec features
does_not_prove: The docs say nothing about how spec decode interacts with prefix caching, chunked prefill, preemption or async scheduling. Those rules live only in code and issues
bearing: context: the feature surface is wide, but the systems interactions are undocumented

title: Dynamic Speculative Decoding (vLLM docs)
quote: K=0 will be used when the concurrency is in range [129, 512], i.e., no draft tokens will be produced.
proves: vLLM dynamic SD is a user-supplied batch-size to K table. It was tested with Eagle, Eagle-3 and DFlash, gets full CUDA graphs only on Model Runner V2, and is auto-disabled with DP>1
does_not_prove: The page gives no method for choosing the table and no numbers. It does not use acceptance or context length
bearing: supports: adaptive speculation-length control is still a static table. threatens: a plain K-vs-batch idea

title: Adaptive Verification (vLLM docs)
quote: the highest-scoring slots are admitted until a global budget is spent.
proves: vLLM can score each (request, position) draft slot by survival probability and admit slots up to a per-step token budget. The budget comes from a startup cost model of step cost per shape. It is off by default, needs a confidence head, and has no LoRA, PP or enforce-eager support
does_not_prove: The cost model is profiled at startup on a synthetic 8192-token KV context. It does not track live memory pressure, preemption, or KV occupancy
bearing: threatens: a verification-budget scheduling candidate. Budget-aware verification already exists upstream

title: Per-Request Acceptance Metrics (vLLM docs)
quote: This lets a client compute the mean acceptance length and the accepted-draft-length distribution for an individual request.
proves: vLLM exposes per-request acceptance (histogram of accepted drafts per step, plus optional per-step arrays) for single-sequence requests
does_not_prove: The metrics are client-facing. Nothing feeds them back into scheduling, admission or preemption decisions
bearing: supports: an acceptance-aware scheduler can get its per-request signal from existing metrics

title: [RFC]: Automate Speculative Decoding #4565
quote: Paradoxically, under conditions of high request rates or low speculation accuracy, latency may actually increase.
proves: The vLLM roadmap had three milestones: disable SD, then dynamic proposal length, then runtime-only information with no pre-profiling
does_not_prove: Opened May 2024. The milestone 3 goal (no pre-profiled parameters) is still unmet in 2026 (see E2, E6-E8)
bearing: supports: runtime-adaptive speculation as a long-standing open problem

title: [Performance]: Dynamic speculative decoding causes catastrophic aggregate-throughput collapse under concurrency at the batch-size threshold #49548
quote: 8 concurrent 180-token requests dropped from **~232 tok/s aggregate** (static `num_speculative_tokens: 2`) to **24–157 tok/s**
proves: Switching K by batch size near the threshold made throughput collapse (MTP k=2, GB10). A later comment shows the same with DSpark on the V2 runner with full graphs: at concurrency 5, 128 vs 410 tok/s and 423 vs 121 ms/step
does_not_prove: The root cause is unresolved and the issue is open. It is single-reporter hardware (GB10, H20)
bearing: supports: K switching has a hidden per-step tax. Any adaptive-K candidate must measure transitions, not just steady states

title: [Perf] DSD arms pay a large baseline tax vs no-spec under production defaults #49986
quote: At ctx=400, the DSD-mode arms are 20-31% slower than no-spec.
proves: At c=256 on an H100 with Gemma-4-31B, every arm with a speculative_config lost to no-spec at short context (static K=3: -21% at ctx 400). Static K=3 beat no-spec only at ctx 4000 (+10%). Part of the cause is the PIECEWISE CUDA-graph override
does_not_prove: One model and GPU. The K=0 tier still carries a loaded drafter and its KV. The memory share of the tax is not separated out
bearing: supports: the cost of keeping spec enabled at K=0 (drafter KV, graphs) is a real resource question

title: [RFC]: Context-length-aware speculative token scheduling #48627
quote: The batch-only rule "speculation stops paying at high batch" is a short-context artifact, not a general property.
proves: On Gemma-4-31B MTP on an H100, the best-K gain fell from 1.79x at concurrency 30 to 1.00x at 128 for short context. The author proposes keying K on (batch, context)
does_not_prove: The author retracted the long-context gain ratios as warm-up biased (correction dated 2026-08-31). Only the short-context crossover stands
bearing: supports: the crossover depends on context length and KV state, not batch alone. Methodology traps are documented

title: [Feature]: Restore length-based speculation skip or per-request speculative decoding control in V1 #52258
quote: long-document summarization (20K–73K Chinese meeting transcripts) collapses to 5–8% acceptance, making speculation net-negative
proves: On real mixed traffic (EAGLE-3/DFlash), short prompts get 1.6-1.8x but long prompts get 5-8% acceptance. V1 lost V0's per-length skip, and no per-request off switch exists
does_not_prove: This is a user report from one deployment with no controlled study
bearing: supports: per-request spec on/off and admission. Production wants to turn spec off per request

title: [Bug]: why does enabling MTP speculative decoding actually reduce the prefix cache hit rate? #38182
quote: Prefix cache hit rate: around 71%
proves: On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with 5500-token fixed prefixes, the prefix-cache hit rate fell from about 92% to about 71% when MTP k=1 was enabled (EAGLE last-block drop on a hybrid model with large blocks)
does_not_prove: The quote is the MTP arm. The no-spec arm reads around 92% in the same body. Maintainers called it expected behavior
bearing: supports: spec decode and prefix caching conflict through draft-KV boundary state

title: [Misc] Warn when EAGLE/MTP speculation costs a large prefix-cache hit #51769
quote: the one-block drop costs **thousands of tokens per request** instead of a nominal 16.
proves: The EAGLE last-block drop is needed for correctness. On hybrid Mamba/GDN models the enlarged attention block makes it a large, silent hit-rate drop that has been reported repeatedly (#38182, #47194, #43559, #50188)
does_not_prove: The PR only adds a warning. It does not change behavior
bearing: context for E12-E14

title: [RFC]: Lookahead-aware prefix-cache hashing for EAGLE-style draft models #50438
quote: It does not prove equality of `x4`, even though `x4` is part of the draft input that produces the final cache entry at that boundary.
proves: The RFC explains precisely why draft KV at a block boundary depends on the next token: the EAGLE/MTP input shift
does_not_prove: It covers local prefix cache keys only. It does not address preemption or swap of draft state
bearing: threatens: a candidate built on draft-KV prefix-reuse correctness, which is now well understood

title: [Core][Spec Decode] Add lookahead-aware prefix cache hashing for EAGLE-style draft models #50897
quote: Greedy output cannot reveal a wrong draft KV (the target verifies every draft), so the check compares the KV itself.
proves: Putting the lookahead token into the block hash raised hit rate from 72.7% to 85.0% and throughput from 9.09 to 12.43 req/s (+37%) on Qwen3.6-27B MTP k=4, GB200, with unchanged acceptance. A stale-draft-KV negative control gave max abs diff 7.55-14.53, against 0.09-0.29 for correct reuse. It also covers the Offloading, Nixl and Mooncake connectors
does_not_prove: The PR is open and was split (E14). Multi-module MTP keeps the drop
bearing: threatens: the prefix-cache plus draft-KV gap is being closed. supports: wrong draft KV is silent, so detection needs KV-level checks

title: [Core][Spec Decode] Lookahead block hashes for EAGLE prefix caching #61589
quote: EAGLE-family drafters write the draft KV at a block's last position from the token after the block, so `main` drops the last matched block on every hit.
proves: Part 1 of #50897, opened 2026-10-14. It covers local prefix cache only. KV-connector support is a stacked part 2. 1,184 CPU unit tests passed
does_not_prove: The GPU benchmarks have not been re-run on the split. It is unmerged as of 2026-10-20
bearing: threatens: the same as E13. This is active work in the last week

title: [Core][Eagle] Fix prefix cache efficiency in prefill phase #44986
quote: Short input (e.g., 2000 tokens, prefix repeat rate 80%，block_size=1536): prefix cache completely failed
proves: With block_size 1536 (hybrid), EAGLE's drop made prefix caching fail fully for short prompts. The PR proposes skipping the drop in prefill
does_not_prove: Results are only in an attached docx. The PR is open, and its reasoning conflicts with E12's (draft KV is written during prefill too)
bearing: context: several competing fixes, so correctness is subtle

title: [Bug]: DFlash2 speculative decoding acceptance permanently collapses to 0% right after prefix cache hit rate goes positive #58894
quote: the drafter keeps proposing tokens every step, but literally none are ever accepted again, for the remainder of the server's uptime.
proves: When the drafter's KV group is not identified, a prefix hit leaves draft state wrong. Acceptance went from 36.9% to 0.0% and stayed there while drafting continued (Qwen3.5 hybrid GDN + DFlash2, Orin)
does_not_prove: Single report on edge hardware with a likely config root cause (no eagle group flagged)
bearing: supports: an acceptance-collapse watchdog or auto-disable. Silent draft-state corruption after cache reuse

title: [RFC]: Suffix decoding on GPU (suffix_gpu) compatible with async scheduling #51788
quote: the CPU suffix tree needs the committed host token ids each step, and under async scheduling the scheduler runs one step ahead of the worker
proves: In-tree suffix decoding forces async scheduling off. The RFC proposes a GPU-resident suffix index with a cross-request global index (at most 532 MB VRAM in the largest config tested)
does_not_prove: It is an RFC with an external package and is unmerged. The suffix-tree memory budget and eviction policy are left as knobs
bearing: supports: suffix tree and n-gram pool as a managed memory tier (GPU or CPU)

title: [RFC]: Preemption victim-selection extension point (least-computed-first) #54644
quote: Both ignore how much work a request has already done
proves: V1 preemption is recompute-only. The recompute tax reaches about 79% in a forced sweep and 10-23% in realistic online serving. The RFC proposes an lcf victim policy and a pluggable select_victim over read-only features
does_not_prove: The proposed RunningView features (computed, cached, arrival, priority, scheduled) contain no spec state: no acceptance rate, draft KV size or lookahead
bearing: supports: spec-aware preemption victim choice is a gap (the preemption lens)

title: [RFC]: Disaggregated Speculative Decoding with Standalone Parallel Draft Model #42109
quote: a 1B–8B draft can add 10–30% to per-step latency on the target GPUs
proves: Their internal POC moves the drafter to separate GPUs (N:M verify:draft servers, a speculation cache with geometric fan-out, dedicated KV blocks per verify server). It reports about 1.4x TPOT against co-located spec decode at the same GPU budget
does_not_prove: Internal POC, not upstream. It says nothing on draft-server failure, migration, or draft KV consistency when a verify server preempts
bearing: supports and threatens: draft placement and migration. Disaggregated drafting is being explored

title: [RFC]: Dynamic Speculation Length (DSL) with Confidence-Threshold Early Exit #36657
quote: the exit condition uses the batch-mean confidence, not the minimum
proves: It proposed a per-step draft early exit on batch-mean confidence. The output stays zero-padded to full K so that scheduler and KV see a fixed shape
does_not_prove: Closed. The fixed shape means KV lookahead stays reserved for max K even on early exit
bearing: context: dynamic K does not shrink reserved spec KV

title: [Bug] EAGLE speculative decoding defeats radix prefix reuse for multi-turn traffic #32459 (SGLang)
quote: Enabling EAGLE speculative decoding collapses radix prefix reuse for multi-turn agentic traffic
proves: On multi-turn OpenHands replay (GLM 744B NVFP4, 8xB200), the deep-prompt cache hit fell from 97% to 40-53% with EAGLE, input throughput from 43,981 to 12,881-16,811 tok/s, and TTFT p50 rose from 0.54 to 2.15-2.68 s
does_not_prove: The root cause is unknown (possibly a defensive bypass after a NaN crash, #19796). It is one model
bearing: supports: the spec plus prefix-cache conflict also exists in SGLang, with a large cost on agentic workloads

title: [Bug] NGRAM speculative decoding corrupts radix-cached KV with the overlap scheduler when requests end on a stop token #44997 (SGLang)
quote: Greedy speculative decoding should be lossless, so this is silent corruption.
proves: A trailing NGRAM verify step for a finishing request likely writes KV into or over radix-cached prefixes under the overlap scheduler. On 0.5.22, 3/192 greedy outputs were wrong. It was found with exact-answer synthetic-weight probes
does_not_prove: The mechanism is probable, not proven. EOS endings were not measured
bearing: supports: rejected or speculative KV versus shared-cache isolation under async overlap is a real correctness risk

title: Speculative Decoding (SGLang docs)
quote: The overlap scheduler currently only supports `--speculative-eagle-topk 1`
proves: SGLang SpecV2 overlaps the CPU scheduling of the next draft with GPU verify, but only for chain drafts (topk=1). NGRAM disables the overlap scheduler and mixed chunked prefill
does_not_prove: The docs have no radix-cache rules and no automatic spec disable by batch size
bearing: context: overlap or async scheduling and tree drafts do not yet compose

title: From research to production: Accelerate OSS LLM with EAGLE-3 on Vertex (LMSYS)
quote: gives us an additional 10% - 20% speedup across the board
proves: In Google Vertex production with SGLang, EAGLE-3 gives a 2-3x decode speedup. The overlap scheduler (Draft, Verify, Draft Extend, with FutureMap) adds 10-20%. TTFT can increase
does_not_prove: No acceptance numbers on production traffic. No batch-size breakdown
bearing: context: production uses overlap scheduling. A TTFT cost is acknowledged

title: SpecForge v0.3.0: a Unified Disaggregated and Colocated Speculative Decoding Stack (LMSYS)
quote: Captured hidden states can be large.
proves: Drafter training captures target hidden states from SGLang prefill servers and moves them through Mooncake. Training on non-target text makes acceptance saturate below what target-generated data gives
does_not_prove: No sizes or bandwidth for hidden-state transport. No serving-time drift measurement
bearing: supports: hidden-state features as a storage and transport tier (the caching lens)

title: Speculative Decoding (TensorRT-LLM docs)
quote: There is currently no way to dynamically disable speculation, thus speed ups are only observable at low batch sizes.
proves: TensorRT-LLM supports MTP, Eagle3, NGram, DraftTarget, PARD, DFlash and SA. Every request gets a draft of max_draft_len, and speculation cannot be disabled at runtime
does_not_prove: The docs do not discuss KV rewind for rejected tokens or KV reuse with drafts
bearing: supports: runtime spec on/off and admission is missing in a major engine

title: Speculative Decoding (llama.cpp docs)
quote: Currently, a single hash pool is shared across all server slots, so different requests can benefit from each other.
proves: llama-server supports a draft model and several n-gram history methods. ngram-mod shares one hash pool across slots. External n-gram statistics can be loaded from files
does_not_prove: Nothing on pool size limits, eviction, or persistence across restarts
bearing: supports: an n-gram pool as shared, persistable state (the checkpoint and caching lenses)

title: SuffixDecoding at Production Scale with Arctic Inference and vLLM (Snowflake)
quote: At high concurrency levels (e.g., 64 requests), speculation overhead began to dominate runtime.
proves: CPU suffix speculation costs 20-30 us per token and scales linearly. At concurrency 64 it was worse than n-gram until a hashmap (3.4x) and two-level list (2.2x) fix, leaving about 10% overhead. 1.96-3.12x on BlazeEdit, 1.0-1.28x on SpecBench
does_not_prove: The memory section mentions eviction with no size limit or policy. No real-traffic acceptance numbers
bearing: supports: suffix-tree memory and CPU cost as a managed resource at high concurrency

title: ATLAS: adaptive-learning speculator system (Together AI)
quote: Put simply, *a static speculator cannot keep up*.
proves: A static speculator plus a lightweight online-adapted speculator plus a confidence-aware controller that sets lookahead. RL acceptance rose from below 10% to above 80% over 1.4k steps. Up to 500 TPS on DeepSeek-V3.1 (batch 1, B200)
does_not_prove: Nothing on memory or KV cost of two speculators, behavior at high batch, or the adaptive state's lifecycle (checkpoint, migration)
bearing: supports: acceptance drifts in production. Adaptive speculator state is new serving state

title: When RL Meets Adaptive Speculative Training: A Unified Training-Serving System (Aurora)
quote: continuously learning a speculator directly from live inference traces
proves: Aurora trains the speculator online from live traces with hot-swapped updates and no service interruption. It reports 1.5x day-0 speedup and an extra 1.25x over a static speculator. It argues speedup cannot be inferred from acceptance rate alone
does_not_prove: Abstract only. Hot-swap consistency for in-flight draft KV and hidden states is not described there
bearing: supports: speculator hot-swap and in-flight draft state as a live-migration question

title: Accelerating PayPal's Commerce Agent with Speculative Decoding: An Empirical Study on EAGLE3 with Fine-Tuned Nemotron Models
quote: acceptance rates remain stable at approximately 35.5% for gamma=3 across all conditions.
proves: On a production agent workload, EAGLE3 acceptance was about 35.5% (gamma=3) and about 25% (gamma=5), flat across concurrency 1-32. Throughput +22-49%
does_not_prove: Concurrency only up to 32 and one workload. No time-series drift
bearing: threatens: acceptance does not degrade with load. supports: real-traffic acceptance is far below benchmark

title: FireOptimizer: Customizing latency and quality for your production inference workload (Fireworks)
quote: When using FireOptimizer, we achieved 76% hit rate with a 2x speed increase.
proves: A generic draft model got a 29% hit rate on a customer workload and made latency 1.5x worse. A workload-tuned draft got 76% and 2x
does_not_prove: A 2024 vendor anecdote with one workload
bearing: negative result: a mismatched drafter is net-negative in production

title: Introducing our Speculative Decoding Engine Builder integration (Baseten)
quote: Our integration is useful for any low-batch, latency-sensitive application
proves: Baseten positions draft-model SD for low batch. It warns that under high load the draft model becomes a bottleneck and needs careful GPU memory split (example kv fraction 0.62)
does_not_prove: No runtime toggle. No acceptance data
bearing: supports: the drafter's memory share against target KV as a sizing problem

title: Looking back at speculative decoding (Google Research)
quote: Speculative decoding enables AI Overviews in Google Search to produce results faster than before
proves: Google uses SD in production, including AI Overviews
does_not_prove: No production numbers and no batch-size discussion
bearing: context only

title: Blackwell Breaks the 1,000 TPS/User Barrier With Meta's Llama 4 Maverick (NVIDIA)
quote: Based on NVIDIA’s experiments below, draft-length=3 provides the best speed-up.
proves: EAGLE3 with draft length 3 is best for single-user latency on B200 (over 1000 TPS per user)
does_not_prove: Latency-focused. Does not say whether SD is used in the 72k TPS max-throughput config
bearing: context: production SD is tuned for latency, not throughput

title: Speculative Decoding: Performance or Illusion?
proves: A systematic study of SD in vLLM: verification dominates execution time, acceptance varies widely by position, request and dataset, and there are large gaps to theoretical bounds
does_not_prove: The fetch tool would not return the abstract verbatim and the PDF was too large, so the quote is empty. No preemption or memory-pressure analysis is visible in the abstract
bearing: supports: verification budget is the main resource

title: SPEED-Bench: A Unified and Diverse Benchmark for Speculative Decoding
quote: SD performance is inherently data-dependent, meaning that diverse and representative workloads are essential
proves: NVIDIA's benchmark finds that synthetic inputs overestimate real throughput and that the optimal draft length depends on batch size
does_not_prove: The abstract gives no numbers. The 23% figure seen in a secondary blog is unverified
bearing: methodology: experiments need real-text workloads, not random tokens

title: Disaggregated Inference design (AWS Neuron vLLM)
quote: runs spec decoding to generate the draft KV cache, so both are available to the decode side.
proves: In Neuron vLLM PD disaggregation with Eagle3, the prefill server produces both target and draft KV for the decode side
does_not_prove: No transfer mechanism, cost, or hidden-state handling is described
bearing: supports: draft KV and features in PD transfer is barely documented (the migration lens)

title: Speeding up LLM inference with P-EAGLE in vLLM and Speculators (Red Hat)
quote: Every model and workload is different.
proves: P-EAGLE (Amazon) drafts several tokens in one forward pass. Training is supported in Speculators v0.6.0. Average acceptance length is 3.044 on Qwen3-8B
does_not_prove: No speedup numbers, nothing on high concurrency, and nothing on inference KV or slot costs. In code it needs K-1 extra slots per request (see e-code.md section 4)
bearing: context: parallel drafters raise per-request slot and budget cost
